_meta.description: Opening mistake patterns — position-specific golden rules

italian_two_knights_d5.name: Two Knights Defense — Premature d5
italian_two_knights_d5.condition: White knight on f3, not Ng5
italian_two_knights_d5.explanation: In the Two Knights Defense, d5 is premature when White hasn't played Ng5. After exd5, Black loses central control and faces tactical problems.
italian_two_knights_d5.why_bad: After exd5 Nxd5, Black's center crumbles. The e5 pawn becomes weak.
italian_two_knights_d5.why_good: d6 supports the e5 pawn, keeps the center solid, and prepares Be7 + O-O.
italian_two_knights_d5.rule: In the Italian/Two Knights, d5 is only good AFTER Ng5. Play d6 first.

italian_giuoco_piano_d5.name: Giuoco Piano — Premature d5
italian_giuoco_piano_d5.explanation: In the Giuoco Piano, d5 gives up the center. d6 is the main line — solid and flexible.
italian_giuoco_piano_d5.why_bad: d5 opens the position when you're not fully developed. White gets active play.
italian_giuoco_piano_d5.why_good: d6 maintains tension, supports e5, and allows flexible development.
italian_giuoco_piano_d5.rule: In the Italian Game, keep the center solid with d6 unless you have a specific tactical reason for d5.

sicilian_premature_d5.name: Sicilian Defense — Premature d5
sicilian_premature_d5.explanation: In the Sicilian, Black should play d6 first to support the c5 pawn. d5 is premature.
sicilian_premature_d5.why_bad: After exd5, Black has no central pawns and White controls the center.
sicilian_premature_d5.why_good: d6 prepares a solid structure. d5 comes later after proper preparation.
sicilian_premature_d5.rule: In the Sicilian, play d6 first. Prepare d5 with pieces, not rush it.

sicilian_najdorf_premature_e5.name: Sicilian Najdorf — Premature e5
sicilian_najdorf_premature_e5.explanation: In the Najdorf, e5 looks active but it weakens d5 permanently. e6 keeps flexibility.
sicilian_najdorf_premature_e5.why_bad: e5 drives the knight away but creates a permanent hole on d5 for White's pieces.
sicilian_najdorf_premature_e5.why_good: e6 controls d5, keeps the position flexible, and prepares Be7 development.
sicilian_najdorf_premature_e5.rule: In the Najdorf, e5 creates a permanent d5 weakness. Prefer e6 unless you know the specific line.

french_attack_chain.name: French Defense — Wrong Pawn Chain Attack
french_attack_chain.explanation: In the French, attack the BASE of the pawn chain (d4) with c5, not the HEAD (e5) with f6.
french_attack_chain.why_bad: f6 attacks the strong part of the chain. After exf6, Black's kingside is weakened.
french_attack_chain.why_good: c5 attacks d4, the base. If White doesn't defend properly, the whole chain collapses.
french_attack_chain.rule: In the French, attack the pawn chain base with c5, not the head with f6.

french_exchange_passive_play.name: French Exchange — Passive Development
french_exchange_passive_play.explanation: In the Exchange French, Black should develop actively. Taking back exd5 is fine, but the key is to then develop the bishop actively.
french_exchange_passive_play.why_bad: Recapturing passively and then playing e6/Be7 gives you a cramped, lifeless position.
french_exchange_passive_play.why_good: Developing actively with Bd6, Nf6, O-O gives Black equal chances in an open game.
french_exchange_passive_play.rule: In the Exchange French, develop actively. The open center favors the side that develops faster.

caro_kann_main_line.name: Caro-Kann — Passive e6 Instead of dxe4
caro_kann_main_line.explanation: In the main line Caro-Kann, capture dxe4 to challenge White's center. e6 is passive.
caro_kann_main_line.why_bad: e6 blocks the light-squared bishop and gives White a space advantage.
caro_kann_main_line.why_good: dxe4 forces White to recapture, then Bf5 develops with tempo.
caro_kann_main_line.rule: In the Caro-Kann, capture dxe4 and develop Bf5 — that's the whole point of the opening.

queens_gambit_grab_c4.name: Queen's Gambit — Grabbing c4 Pawn
queens_gambit_grab_c4.explanation: In the Queen's Gambit, accepting with dxc4 gives up the center. e6 maintains central control.
queens_gambit_grab_c4.why_bad: After dxc4, White plays e4 and dominates the center. The c4 pawn is hard to hold.
queens_gambit_grab_c4.why_good: e6 supports d5, prepares Nf6 and Bd6. Black keeps equal chances.
queens_gambit_grab_c4.rule: In the Queen's Gambit, don't grab the pawn unless you know the theory. e6 or c6 are safe.

london_system_passive_bg4.name: London System — Passive Bg4 Pin
london_system_passive_bg4.explanation: Against the London, challenge the center with c5 instead of pinning with Bg4.
london_system_passive_bg4.why_bad: Bg4 doesn't challenge White's setup. White plays e3 and has a comfortable position.
london_system_passive_bg4.why_good: c5 attacks d4 immediately and challenges White's central control.
london_system_passive_bg4.rule: Against the London, play c5 early to challenge the center. Don't just develop passively.

ruy_lopez_premature_nxe4.name: Ruy Lopez — Premature Nxe4
ruy_lopez_premature_nxe4.explanation: Nxe4 in the Ruy Lopez looks tempting but White gets strong compensation after d4.
ruy_lopez_premature_nxe4.why_bad: After d4, White opens the center with a huge lead in development. Black struggles to hold.
ruy_lopez_premature_nxe4.why_good: a6 asks the bishop a question — it must decide where to go. This is the main line.
ruy_lopez_premature_nxe4.rule: In the Ruy Lopez, play a6 to question the bishop. Don't grab e4 without preparation.

ruy_lopez_early_d5.name: Ruy Lopez — Early d5 Break
ruy_lopez_early_d5.explanation: d5 is premature in the Ruy Lopez. Black needs more preparation before this central break.
ruy_lopez_early_d5.why_bad: After exd5 Nxd5, White has Nxe5 winning a pawn with an attack.
ruy_lopez_early_d5.why_good: a6 first forces the bishop to commit, then prepare d5 with proper support.
ruy_lopez_early_d5.rule: In the Ruy Lopez, prepare d5 with a6 and b5 first. Don't rush central breaks.

scotch_game_recapture_qxd4.name: Scotch Game — Recapture with Queen
scotch_game_recapture_qxd4.condition: Scotch Game, Black to respond to d4
scotch_game_recapture_qxd4.explanation: In the Scotch, take the pawn with exd4. Qh4 looks aggressive but it's a beginner trap.
scotch_game_recapture_qxd4.why_bad: Qh4 puts the queen out early where it can be attacked. White gains tempo with Nc3.
scotch_game_recapture_qxd4.why_good: exd4 is the normal response. After Nxd4, Black can develop with Nf6 or Bc5.
scotch_game_recapture_qxd4.rule: Don't bring your queen out early to attack. Develop pieces first.

kings_indian_passive_d6_e5.name: King's Indian — Missing e5 Break
kings_indian_passive_d6_e5.explanation: In the King's Indian, e5 is Black's key break. Delaying it lets White dominate the center.
kings_indian_passive_d6_e5.why_bad: Bg4 doesn't challenge the center. White can play h3 and gain time.
kings_indian_passive_d6_e5.why_good: e5 is the thematic break. It challenges White's center and activates the g7 bishop.
kings_indian_passive_d6_e5.rule: In the King's Indian, play e5. This is the whole point of the opening.

slav_defense_premature_bf5.name: Slav Defense — Premature Bf5
slav_defense_premature_bf5.explanation: In the Slav, Bf5 before Nf6 allows White to play Qb3 targeting b7 and d5.
slav_defense_premature_bf5.why_bad: After Qb3, Black must defend both b7 and d5 simultaneously — very awkward.
slav_defense_premature_bf5.why_good: Nf6 develops a piece and keeps all options open for the bishop later.
slav_defense_premature_bf5.rule: In the Slav, develop Nf6 before Bf5. Don't leave d5 and b7 undefended.

vienna_game_premature_f5.name: Vienna Game — Premature f5
vienna_game_premature_f5.explanation: f5 in the Vienna looks aggressive but weakens Black's king and gives White attacking chances.
vienna_game_premature_f5.why_bad: After exf5, Black's e5 pawn is weak and the kingside is exposed.
vienna_game_premature_f5.why_good: Nf6 develops naturally, defends e5 indirectly, and keeps the position balanced.
vienna_game_premature_f5.rule: Against the Vienna, develop naturally with Nf6. Don't weaken your kingside with f5.

scandinavian_early_queen_Qd8.name: Scandinavian — Retreating Queen to d8
scandinavian_early_queen_Qd8.explanation: Retreating the queen to d8 wastes a tempo. Qa5 is the main line keeping the queen active.
scandinavian_early_queen_Qd8.why_bad: Qd8 loses a full tempo — you're back to the starting position but White has a free move.
scandinavian_early_queen_Qd8.why_good: Qa5 keeps the queen active while planning to develop with Nf6, Bf5, and c6.
scandinavian_early_queen_Qd8.rule: In the Scandinavian, Qa5 is the main line. Keep the queen active, not passive.

philidor_passive_be7.name: Philidor Defense — Passive Be7
philidor_passive_be7.explanation: Be7 is too passive in the Philidor. Nf6 develops with tempo and keeps options open.
philidor_passive_be7.why_bad: Be7 blocks the queen, doesn't attack anything, and makes the position cramped.
philidor_passive_be7.why_good: Nf6 attacks e4, develops with tempo, and keeps the option of Bg4 or Be7 later.
philidor_passive_be7.rule: In the Philidor, develop knights before bishops. Nf6 first, then decide on the bishop.

pirc_ignore_center.name: Pirc Defense — Ignoring the Center
pirc_ignore_center.explanation: In the Pirc, the g7 bishop is the heart of the defense. Delaying Bg7 lets White build an overwhelming center.
pirc_ignore_center.why_bad: a6 doesn't develop a piece or challenge the center. White gets e5 with a huge advantage.
pirc_ignore_center.why_good: Bg7 completes the fianchetto, puts pressure on d4, and prepares O-O.
pirc_ignore_center.rule: In the Pirc, fianchetto the bishop immediately. Bg7 is the whole point of the setup.

dutch_defense_early_g5.name: Dutch Defense — Premature g5
dutch_defense_early_g5.explanation: g5 is a premature kingside advance. e6 is the solid choice building a strong center.
dutch_defense_early_g5.why_bad: g5 weakens the kingside drastically. White can exploit with Qc2 and e4.
dutch_defense_early_g5.why_good: e6 supports d5, prepares Be7 and O-O. Solid and principled.
dutch_defense_early_g5.rule: In the Dutch, don't push kingside pawns before castling. Complete development first.

benoni_passive_e6.name: Benoni — Missing c5 Break
benoni_passive_e6.explanation: In the Benoni, Black must play d6 to establish the pawn structure, not block the bishop with e6.
benoni_passive_e6.why_bad: e6 leads to a passive French-like structure without the normal French advantages.
benoni_passive_e6.why_good: d6 prepares the classic Benoni structure with e5/e6 flexibility and g6-Bg7 fianchetto.
benoni_passive_e6.rule: In the Benoni, play d6 to keep the Benoni structure. e6 loses the character of the opening.

nimzo_indian_passive_d5.name: Nimzo-Indian — Passive d5
nimzo_indian_passive_d5.explanation: In the Nimzo-Indian, castling is more flexible than committing to d5 immediately.
nimzo_indian_passive_d5.why_bad: d5 commits the pawn structure too early. After cxd5 exd5, the isolated d-pawn can be weak.
nimzo_indian_passive_d5.why_good: O-O keeps all options open. You can play d5, c5, or b6 depending on White's setup.
nimzo_indian_passive_d5.rule: In the Nimzo-Indian, castle first and keep your options flexible.

english_passive_d5.name: English Opening — Premature d5
english_passive_d5.explanation: Against the English, e5 grabs central space. d5 can be premature — after cxd5, Black must recapture awkwardly.
english_passive_d5.why_bad: After cxd5 Qxd5, the queen is exposed. After cxd5 Nf6, White can play d4 with a good center.
english_passive_d5.why_good: e5 grabs space, controls d4, and leads to a reversed Sicilian where Black is fine.
english_passive_d5.rule: Against 1.c4, consider e5 to grab central space. Don't rush d5.

generic_early_queen_attack.name: Early Queen Sortie
generic_early_queen_attack.condition: Queen moves before move 5 without specific tactical reason
generic_early_queen_attack.explanation: Bringing the queen out early exposes it to attack. Each tempo lost retreating the queen is a free developing move for the opponent.
generic_early_queen_attack.why_bad: The queen can be chased with tempo, giving your opponent free development.
generic_early_queen_attack.why_good: Develop minor pieces first (knights and bishops), then castle, then connect rooks.
generic_early_queen_attack.rule: Don't bring the queen out early. Develop knights, bishops, castle — then the queen finds its place.

generic_no_castling_by_move_10.name: Delayed Castling
generic_no_castling_by_move_10.condition: King still in center after move 10
generic_no_castling_by_move_10.explanation: Leaving the king in the center past move 10 is dangerous. The center can open up at any time.
generic_no_castling_by_move_10.why_bad: An uncastled king is vulnerable to center attacks, discovered checks, and sacrifices.
generic_no_castling_by_move_10.why_good: Castling connects your rooks, tucks the king away, and activates a rook.
generic_no_castling_by_move_10.rule: Castle before move 10. If you haven't castled by move 10, something went wrong.

generic_moving_same_piece_twice.name: Moving Same Piece Twice
generic_moving_same_piece_twice.condition: Same piece moved twice in first 8 moves without being attacked
generic_moving_same_piece_twice.explanation: Moving the same piece twice in the opening wastes time. Each move should develop a NEW piece.
generic_moving_same_piece_twice.why_bad: Every wasted tempo is a free developing move for your opponent. They'll have more pieces in play.
generic_moving_same_piece_twice.why_good: Develop a different piece each move: knight, knight, bishop, bishop, castle.
generic_moving_same_piece_twice.rule: Each opening move should develop a NEW piece. Don't move the same piece twice unless forced.

generic_pawn_hunting_with_queen.name: Queen Pawn Hunting
generic_pawn_hunting_with_queen.condition: Queen captures wing pawns while pieces are undeveloped
generic_pawn_hunting_with_queen.explanation: Capturing wing pawns with the queen while your pieces sit undeveloped is a classic beginner mistake.
generic_pawn_hunting_with_queen.why_bad: While your queen chases pawns, your opponent develops pieces and attacks your queen.
generic_pawn_hunting_with_queen.why_good: Focus on development. A pawn isn't worth falling behind 3-4 tempi in development.
generic_pawn_hunting_with_queen.rule: Never go pawn hunting with the queen in the opening. Development beats material at this stage.

petrov_defense_passive_nxe4.name: Petrov Defense — Wrong Capture Sequence
petrov_defense_passive_nxe4.explanation: Nxe5 looks natural but Black has the tricky Nxe4 response. d3 is the quiet but strong choice.
petrov_defense_passive_nxe4.why_bad: After Nxe5 d6, White must retreat and Black equalizes easily with active play.
petrov_defense_passive_nxe4.why_good: d3 protects e4 solidly and prepares a slow but steady buildup.
petrov_defense_passive_nxe4.rule: In the Petrov, the simple d3 is often stronger than the aggressive Nxe5.

grunfeld_hold_center.name: Grunfeld — Wrong Center Strategy
grunfeld_hold_center.explanation: In the Grunfeld, White should capture cxd5 to establish a big center with e4.
grunfeld_hold_center.why_bad: Nf3 is too slow and lets Black equalize with standard development.
grunfeld_hold_center.why_good: cxd5 Nxd5 e4 gives White the massive center that defines the Grunfeld battle.
grunfeld_hold_center.rule: Against the Grunfeld, build the big center with cxd5 and e4. That's your whole strategy.
